                                     PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                        § PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                     §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                  §            OF TEXAS


      COMMENTS OF MONARCH ENERGY DEVELOPMENT LLC ON STAFF’s
         QUESTIONS AND DISCUSSION DRAFT OF NEW 16 TAC §25.194

       COMES NOW Monarch Energy Development LLC (Monarch) and files these comments

regarding Commission Staff’s Discussion Draft proposing a new 16 Texas Administrative Code

(TAC) §25.194 relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards, which would set forth the

standards and criteria for an electric utility to interconnect a large load customer to the ERCOT

transmission network. Monarch is also providing comments in response to Commission Staff’s

Questions posed with the Discussion Draft. Commission Staff requested comments be filed by

December 19, 2025, so these comments are timely filed.

       Monarch develops industrial sites that can host a range of assets, including large loads.

Monarch Energy secures land, power, water rights, designs, equipment, and other critical

development items necessary for bringing energy assets to communities. Monarch streamlines the

development timeline for industrial development including hyperscalers, cloud providers, and

enterprise operators.

       A significant portion of data center capacity is developed by independent data center

developers and operators that provide the physical infrastructure necessary to support future end

users. These independent developers are responsible for managing large load interconnection

processes, including submitting interconnection requests, procuring equipment, coordinating with

transmission service providers, and bearing substantial up-front financial and operational risk

associated with interconnecting large loads to the transmission system.
        This development model benefits the market by producing projects that are ready for

market deployment and can be offered to a broad spectrum of creditworthy end users once

infrastructure and interconnection milestones are accomplished. Consequently, the entities bearing

the primary financial, operational, and interconnection risks associated with large load

development often differ from the ultimate beneficiaries of the constructed and occupied projects.

This distinction is crucial when evaluating and implementing new regulations concerning the

interconnection of large loads, including stipulations related to security, risk allocation, and refund

mechanisms under Senate Bill 6.


       RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S QUESTIONS

1. Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load customer
   is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request? If so, how should the
   commission define those parameters?

       Monarch recommends that the Commission define “substantially similar interconnection

requests” using objective load attributes, such as load magnitude, ramp rate, flexibility attributes,

voltage level, and point of interconnection, because these are the characteristics that directly

impact system reliability and transmission planning. Importantly, these parameters are the

characteristics that determine whether an interconnection affects system reliability or requires

transmission upgrades, which ensures that the classification remains focused on engineering, not

business models. Location is also a key driver of transmission planning needs, ensuring the

definition aligns with ERCOT’s reliability modeling, but for purposes of determining whether a

large load customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request, identification of

the load zone of another project should be sufficient without having to divulge the exact

coordinates of the project. Disclosure of the load zone of the project would be consistent with the

information ERCOT will require for implementation of NPRR 1267, Large Load Interconnection


                                                                          Monarch Comments - Page 2
 Status Report, which added ERCOT Protocol Section 3.2.7, Large Load Interconnection Status

Report (currently greyboxed). This new requirement provides a list of data that ERCOT must

include in its monthly Status Report on large load interconnections in ERCOT. Since ERCOT will

need to collect the underlying information from TSPs, it is appropriate for each TSP to receive this

information identifying the load zone of the interconnection of the other potential project, but more

detailing information is not necessary for this purpose.

        Monarch further recommends that the definition remains technology-neutral and not

classify requests based on customer type or industry sector. Such factors do not materially affect

system reliability, and including them could distort competitive markets, deter capital investment,

and risk subjecting certain industries to discriminatory treatment. Moreover, using technology

specific definitions to determine what are similar interconnection requests risks adding subjective

considerations and creating a dynamic where the Commission is picking winners or favoring

certain industries.

        A clear, predictable, and technically-grounded approach to this issue will reduce

administrative uncertainty, prevent duplicative studies, improve queue efficiency, and preserve

Texas’s competitiveness for large-load economic development such as datacenters as well as other

industrial facilities. From a datacenter developer’s perspective, regulatory clarity is essential.

Without clear parameters, large load customers may face inconsistent interpretations from utilities,

delays, or duplicative studies, conditions that increase development risk, and undermine Texas’s

attractiveness for data-intensive industries.

2. Proposed subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the disclosure of specific
   information related to a substantially similar request for interconnection and allows a
   large load customer to anonymize competitively sensitive details. Should the commission
   list what is and is not competitively sensitive (e.g., load zone is not competitively sensitive
   information)? If so, what information should and should not be considered competitively



                                                                         Monarch Comments - Page 3
    sensitive such that the interconnecting utility and ERCOT can identify whether there is
   a duplicate request, or a request is unlikely to materialize?

         The Commission should define a clear set of non-sensitive technical data that must be

disclosed to utilities and ERCOT, while preserving the ability of large load customers to anonymize

commercially sensitive information. Technical characteristics that determine system impact, such

as load size, ramp rate, transmission line or node, voltage level, and timing, should always be

disclosed. In addition, details regarding electrical and interconnection characteristics, geographic

and system information, and study related information will allow ERCOT/utility engineers to

evaluate impacts without exposing competitive business strategy. These details also help identify

speculative requests.

         Conversely, business-specific or customer-specific information, including customer

identity, commercial strategy, procurement plans, competitive position, and facility technology,

should be explicitly deemed competitively sensitive and permitted to be anonymized. These

elements do not change the system impact of the interconnection request and should remain

confidential to protect the customer’s competitive position. This approach enables ERCOT and

utilities to identify duplicative or speculative requests without imposing unreasonable disclosure

burdens that would harm Texas’s competitiveness in attracting datacenters and other large electric

loads.

3. Should the commission require a large load customer to notify the interconnecting
   electric utility and ERCOT of any change to information that is initially disclosed in
   response to this rule or only material changes to the information disclosed? If only
   material changes, how should “material change” be defined?

         The Commission should require notification only of “material changes,” defined as

changes that would materially alter the results of interconnection studies or ERCOT’s reliability

assessment. Material changes should include significant variations in load magnitude, in-service



                                                                        Monarch Comments - Page 4
 date shifts outside a defined threshold, changes to load ramping or flexibility characteristics,

relocation of the interconnection point, or meaningful adjustments to onsite generation or storage

that affect net load. A material change standard focuses disclosure on the small set of changes that

actually affect interconnection studies, transmission planning, and ERCOT reliability modeling.

This standard preserves transparency where it matters while enabling efficient project

development.

       Non-material changes, such as internal business decisions, vendor selection, minor design

modifications, or load fluctuations within established tolerances, should not require notification.

This approach ensures ERCOT and utilities receive the information necessary for reliability

planning without imposing excessive reporting burdens that could slow industrial site development

or distort competitive markets.

4. Proposed subsection (k)(1) authorizes an interconnecting electric utility to refund 20%
   of a large load customer’s security after energization and ratably as the large load
   customer meets the milestones identified in the customer’s schedule for phased
   energization of its contracted load. Should the commission standardize the rate for
   refund for reaching milestones identified in the customer’s schedule for phased
   energization (e.g., 20% for each year of operations until the full amount of security is
   refunded)? If so, how should the commission standardize the refund?

       In the discussion draft, Commission Staff has proposed two forms of financial security in

subsections (e)(8) and (h)(8). The Commission’s rules should provide that 100% of a large load

customer’s financial security paid pursuant to subsection (e)(8) is refunded when the customer

pays Contribution in Aid of Construction (CIAC) in an amount that is equal to the interconnecting

utility’s expected costs to interconnect the large load customer. At that point, the customer is

making a significant and enforceable financial commitment to the interconnecting electric utility.

Requiring a customer to maintain financial security pursuant to subsection (e)(8) while

simultaneously posting CIAC payments would result in duplicative financial assurances that



                                                                        Monarch Comments - Page 5
 exceed what is necessary to protect the system or the utility and could unnecessarily constrain

capital required for ongoing construction and operations.

       The refund provisions of subsection (k) are appropriately applied to the financial security

posted pursuant to subsection (h)(8) as that is directly related to the costs to interconnect the large

load customer. For the refund of that financial security, the Commission should exercise caution

in standardizing a fixed refund rate for large load security tied solely to the passage of time or

uniform percentage milestones (e.g., 20% per year). Large load projects, particularly data centers,

advanced manufacturing, and other phased developments, vary significantly in construction

sequencing, capital deployment, operational ramp profiles, and grid impact.

   5. Are changes to the commission’s other substantive rules necessary to align with this
      rulemaking? If so, what changes need to be made to which rules?

       Yes. Targeted conforming changes to the Commission’s transmission interconnection,

planning, and service rules will be necessary to fully align them with this large-load rulemaking.

Rules relating to confidentiality, load resources, and transmission cost recovery also may need

revisions. These changes should ensure consistent definitions, avoid conflicting obligations, and

clearly recognize that modern datacenters are both large loads and potential reliability resources.

A harmonized framework will reduce regulatory friction, preserve system reliability, and support

continued large-scale investment in Texas.


  COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC PROVISIONS IN THE STAFF’S DISCUSSION DRAFT

       Monarch offers the following specific rule language modifications consistent with the

Comments above in response to the Staff’s questions. Edits are shown as redlines to the Staff’s

proposed language.




                                                                          Monarch Comments - Page 6
 Subsection (b), Definitions.

       Consistent with Monarch’s recommendation in response to Question No. 3, Monarch

recommends adding a new paragraph (b)(10) to define material change, renumbering subsequent

definitions accordingly.

       (10)    Material change – A material change refers to a significant change in facts,
               conditions, or circumstances substantial enough to materially alter the results of
               interconnection studies or ERCOT’s reliability assessment. Examples of material
               changes include significant variations in load magnitude, in-service date changes
               of more than 6 months, significant changes to load ramping or flexibility
               characteristics, relocation of the interconnection point, or meaningful adjustments
               to onsite generation or storage that affect net load.

Subsection (c), Disclosures, and study fee upon receipt of interconnection request.

       Consistent with our responses to Question Nos. 1-3, Monarch offers the following

proposed changes to subsection (c). This language should be mirrored in other subsections of the

rule that have similar language, including subsections (e) and (h).

(c)    Disclosures and study fee upon receipt of interconnection request. Prior to conducting
       a large load interconnection study, the interconnecting electric utility must obtain the
       disclosures and study fee under this subsection from a large load customer seeking to
       interconnect in the electric utility’s retail delivery service area.
       (1)    Project developer or end-use customer. A large load customer must disclose to
              the interconnecting utility whether the customer is a project developer or an end-
              use customer.
       (2)    Site control. A large load customer must demonstrate site control for the proposed
              load location through provision of one of the following property interests to the
              interconnecting electric utility:
              (A)     a legally binding option to purchase or lease for the proposed load location;
              (B)     a signed and executed lease agreement for the proposed load location; or
              (C)     a deed for the proposed load location.
       (3)    Substantially similar interconnection request. A large load customer must
              disclose to the interconnecting electric utility whether the customer is pursuing a
              substantially similar interconnection request for electric service, the approval of
              which would result in the customer materially changing, delaying, or withdrawing
              the interconnection request.
              (A)      A large load customer that is pursuing a substantially similar
                      interconnection request for electric service, the approval of which would
                      result in the customer materially changing, delaying, or withdrawing the


                                                                       Monarch Comments - Page 7
                       interconnection request must disclose the following information to the
                      interconnecting electric utility:
                      (i)     the location, including the load zone, of the substantially similar
                              interconnection request;
                      (ii)    the size load, ramp rate, flexibility attributes, and voltage level of
                              the substantially similar interconnection request;
                      (iii)   the anticipated timing of energization of the substantially similar
                              interconnection request; and
                      (iv)    the interconnecting electric utility for the substantially similar
                              interconnection request.
              (B)     A large load customer that discloses a substantially similar interconnection
                      request under this subsection may anonymize competitively sensitive
                      details, including business-specific or customer-specific information,
                      including customer identity, commercial strategy, procurement plans,
                      competitive position, and facility technology, in its disclosure to the
                      interconnecting electric utility.
              (C)     An interconnecting electric utility must not sell, share, or disclose
                      information submitted to the utility under this subsection other than a
                      disclosure to the commission or ERCOT.
              (D)     A large load customer must notify the utility of any material change to the
                      facts provided under this subsection within 15 business days of the change.

Subsection (k), Terms for refund of financial security for a large load customer that energizes

       For clarity, and consistent with our recommendation in the response to Question No. 4,

Monarch recommends modifying the language in paragraph (k)(1) as follows:

       (1)    After applying the financial security provided pursuant to subsection (h)(8) to any
              amounts owed, the interconnecting electric utility must refund 100% of the security
              when the large load customer posts the CIAC. and ratably as the large load customer
              meets the milestones




                                                                        Monarch Comments - Page 8
                                       CONCLUSION

       Monarch appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and encourages the

Commission to move to formal publication of a proposed rule consistent with these comments.

                                 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

 •   Q1: Monarch recommends that the Commission define “substantially similar
     interconnection requests” using objective load attributes, such as load magnitude, ramp
     rate, flexibility attributes, voltage level, and point of interconnection, because these are the
     characteristics that directly impact system reliability and transmission planning.
     Identification of the load zone of the alternative interconnection request is appropriate, but
     specific coordinates of the location should not be required. The definition should be
     technology-neutral and not business models.

 •   Q2: Technical characteristics that determine system impact, such as load size, ramp rate,
     transmission line or node, voltage level, and timing, should always be disclosed to the
     electric utility. Business-specific or customer-specific information, including customer
     identity, commercial strategy, procurement plans, competitive position, and facility
     technology, should be explicitly deemed competitively sensitive and permitted to be
     anonymized.

 •   Q3: The Commission should require notification only of “material changes,” defined as
     changes that would materially alter the results of interconnection studies or ERCOT’s
     reliability assessment. Material changes should include significant variations in load
     magnitude, in-service date shifts outside a defined threshold, changes to load ramping or
     flexibility characteristics, relocation of the interconnection point, or meaningful
     adjustments to onsite generation or storage that affect net load. Non-material changes, such
     as internal business decisions, vendor selection, minor design modifications, or load
     fluctuations within established tolerances, should not require notification.

 •   Q4: The Commission should adopt a standardized refund structure. We recommend
     refunding 100% percent of the customer’s security paid pursuant to subsection (e)(8) upon
     CIAC posting.

 •   Q5: Targeted conforming changes to the Commission’s transmission interconnection,
     planning, and service rules will be necessary to fully align them with this large-load
     rulemaking. Rules relating to confidentiality, load resources, and transmission cost
     recovery also may need revisions.

 •   Specific language changes: see pages 6-8 for specific recommended edits to subsections
     (b), (c), and (k).

                                 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

 •   Ql: Monarch recommends that the Commission define "substantially similar
     interconnection requests" using obj ective load attributes, such as load magnitude, ramp
     rate, flexibility attributes, voltage level, and point of interconnection, because these are the
     characteristics that directly impact system reliability and transmission planning.
     Identification ofthe load zone of the alternative interconnection request is appropriate, but
     specific coordinates of the location should not be required. The definition should be
     technology-neutral and not business models.

 •   Q2: Technical characteristics that determine system impact, such as load size, ramp rate,
     transmission line or node, voltage level, and timing, should always be disclosed to the
     electric utility. Business-specific or customer-specific information, including customer
     identity, commercial strategy, procurement plans, competitive position, and facility
     technology, should be explicitly deemed competitively sensitive and permitted to be
     anonymized.

 •   Q3: The Commission should require notification only of "material changes," defined as
     changes that would materially alter the results of interconnection studies or ERCOT's
     reliability assessment. Material changes should include significant variations in load
     magnitude, in-service date shifts outside a defined threshold, changes to load ramping or
     flexibility characteristics, relocation of the interconnection point, or meaningful
     adjustments to onsite generation or storage that affect net load. Non-material changes, such
     as internal business decisions, vendor selection, minor design modifications, or load
     fluctuations within established tolerances, should not require notification.

 •   Q4: The Commission should adopt a standardized refund structure. We recommend
     refunding 100% percent of the customer's security paid pursuant to subsection (e)(8) upon
     CIAC posting.

 •   Q5: Targeted conforming changes to the Commission's transmission interconnection,
     planning, and service rules will be necessary to fully align them with this large-load
     rulemaking. Rules relating to confidentiality, load resources, and transmission cost
     recovery also may need revisions.
